discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Cool upper level trough offshore will move inland tonight. Split flow aloft Tuesday ahead of the next system moving inland south of the area Wednesday into Thursday. Upper level ridge over Western Washington Friday. Next system splitting as it moves into the Pacific Northwest over the weekend with most of the energy going into Northern California.
hydrology: The Skokomish River has fallen below flood stage and will continue to recede into this week. No river flooding expected this week in Western Washington.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Cool upper level trough offshore will move inland tonight. Split flow aloft Tuesday ahead of the next system moving inland south of the area Wednesday into Thursday. Upper level ridge over Western Washington Friday. Next system splitting as it moves into the Pacific Northwest over the weekend with most of the energy going into Northern California.

sections.title: Short term (today through Wednesday)
paragraphs: An upper level trough remains offshore today keeping showers in the forecast. Air mass slightly unstable. Shower activity increasing this afternoon as the trough axis approaches the coast and a little daytime heating increases the instablilty. Today will be the coolest day in two weeks with highs only in the lower 50s.
Seas in the upper teens to near 20 feet this morning subsiding to 10 to 14 feet by tonight. High surf advisory has been extended through this afternoon.
Upper level trough axis moving through Western Washington tonight. Shower activity becoming confined to the coast and mountains after midnight. Lows in the mid 30s to lower 40s.

Dry day Tuesday with split flow aloft caused by the deep cool upper level trough and associated front digging south offshore between 130W and 140W. Light surface gradients in the morning combining with plenty of low level moisture to produce areas of fog. Increasing offshore flow in the afternoon as the system offshore gets closer to the coast will help dry out the lower layers of the air mass enough to dissipate the fog. Highs remaining in the lower 50s.

Vertically stacked low offshore moving southeast Tuesday night. Low level offshore flow continuing to increase with the cross cascade gradients getting down to around -6 mb. Low enough to create some breezy easterly winds in the Cascade Foothills. Middle and high level clouds out ahead of the frontal system spreading over the area overnight but not before temperatures have dropped into the mid 30s to lower 40s.

Weather system moving inland south of the area Wednesday. Showers rotating around the low could get as far north as Everett in the afternoon. Best chances for showers will be over the Southwest Interior and Central Coast in the morning. Increasing cloud cover will knock a couple of degrees off the high temperatures with some locations, especially over the southern portion of the area, remaining in the 40s. Highs in the lower 50s elsewhere.

sections.title: Long term (Wednesday night through Sunday)
paragraphs: Upper level low a little further north in the solutions this morning keeping a chance of showers over the Central and Southern Cascades Wednesday evening.

Dry for the most part Thursday but what is left of the upper level low hanging around in the vicinity. Will not be surprised if future runs reintroduce a chance of showers to the southern half Thursday. Upper low kicks off to the east Thursday night with a high amplitude, but narrow, upper level ridge over the area Friday making for a dry day with areas of morning fog. Upper level ridge gets pinched off Friday night as another upper level low drops down from the Gulf of Alaska and takes a position off the coast for the weekend. This feature will bring showers back to the forecast Saturday and Sunday. Snow levels lowering to below pass level over the weekend but at this point not much moisture making it into the area making for light new snow accumulations at best.
Lows in the 30s with the cooler locations getting into the upper 20s Friday and Saturday morning. Highs in the mid 40s to lower 50s. JD/Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Predominantly VFR conditions are expected today through this evening. However, isolated pockets of fog and some isolated showers this morning. Isolated MVFR cigs for coastal airfields as showers continue into the afternoon. Fog is expected to develop overnight into Tuesday morning, first for South Sound and Chehalis River Valley (KOLM), then later spreading into other portions of the Puget Sound resulting in the potential for IFR to LIFR from the early morning hours before dissipating mid-morning.

KSEA...VFR throughout the morning and into the evening. Southerly winds 3-6 kt. Areas of fog looks to develop overnight into Tuesday morning and could encroach upon the terminal, likely dissipating mid-morning Tuesday.
Wolcott

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: More much benign conditions across are waters today (minus seas over the coastal waters). Winds are lighter across all area waters on Monday as high pressure briefly builds over the area. Seas will be around 15-20 ft this morning before gradually decreasing reaching 9- 12 ft by early Tuesday morning. Winds will increase on Tuesday and Tuesday night as a low pressure system passes by off to the west and south. Winds will turn offshore, which may be locally enhanced near the Strait of Juan de Fuca and near Grays Harbor when the wind direction is aligned with the terrain gaps, mainly Tuesday night. This will also push seas back up to 12-15 ft Tuesday night into early Wednesday. SCAs and potential gales may be issued for the coastal waters and Strait of Juan de Fuca.

Calmer conditions will then follow as winds and seas ease during the day Wednesday, with another brief round of high pressure over the area Thursday into early Friday. Another series of systems look to move through the area Friday night into the weekend.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: The Skokomish River has fallen below flood stage and will continue to recede into this week. No river flooding expected this week in Western Washington.
JD

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Unsettled showery weather continues today while a high surf threat lingers. After a temporary return to dry weather on Tuesday, another system undercutting the region to the south swings additional precipitation into the area for Wednesday coupled with snowfall concerns for the Cascade passes. Dry weather (and areas of morning fog) return again to end the work week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Unsettled showery weather continues today while a high surf threat lingers. After a temporary return to dry weather on Tuesday, another system undercutting the region to the south swings additional precipitation into the area for Wednesday coupled with snowfall concerns for the Cascade passes. Dry weather (and areas of morning fog) return again to end the work week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Sunday...Radar observations show scattered shower activity across southwestern Washington and western Oregon this morning with the bulk of the stronger convection just off the coastline, especially north of Tillamook. As we head through the day, these showers likely continue at times as the axis of the upper-level trough passes overhead. It's worth quickly pointing out due to the low level horizontal and vertical shear profile near the coastline early this morning, some of the stronger convective cells have been showing signs of broad rotation on radar. This shear does weaken by midday into the afternoon thanks to the progression of the trough, but we'll still need to monitor for waterspout/funnel potential. Once this trough feature shifts eastward this evening, lingering activity is expected to quickly diminish with dry weather returning overnight. Snow levels hold around 4000ft today but accumulations at pass level will be fleeting given the decent breaks between showers - limited snowfall impacts for those driving across the Cascades.

Then dry conditions are expected through Tuesday afternoon as high pressure briefly passes over the region. Areas of morning valley fog likely make a return with pockets of low visibility possible for those commuting in portions of the Willamette Valley and coastal valleys Tuesday morning. The next weather system then approaches Tuesday night into Wednesday as surface low pressure quickly spins up offshore. Ensemble clusters are still in good agreement with the general track of the system diving south toward California. The question remains how much precipitation to expect with an embedded shortwave and accompanying occluded frontal band lifting northward across the area by Wednesday morning. While precipitation don't appear noteworthy, the airmass will still be on the cooler side when this system hits, and snow levels are forecast to be around 3000-3500 ft Tuesday night into Wednesday. Compared to model guidance yesterday, chances for 2+ inches of snowfall Tuesday night through Wednesday at pass level has increased significantly with a 50-70% chance to exceed this threshold at Willamette/Santiam, 20-25% Government Camp. If you plan to travel across the passes during the middle of the week, chances are looking better you may encounter some winter-like driving conditions. Also of note, offshore easterly winds are expected to increase Tuesday night as pressure gradients tighten in response to the low pressure offshore. East winds will likely be strongest through the Columbia River Gorge into the eastern Portland Metro area with gusts approaching 25-35 mph - locally higher near Corbett and at our other windiest spots.

Ensembles remain in good agreement for another extended dry period Thursday into Friday as we see a brief break between systems. Thanks to the higher pressure moving overhead, lighter winds, and ample surface moisture, morning valley fog likely returns. Uncertainty increases late Friday night into the weekend as the progressive weather pattern returns increasing chances for low pressure systems to develop offshore, and over 70-80% of the 00z EPS members show precipitation returning by Sunday. -99/DH

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Tuesday...Widely scattered post-frontal showers are expected to continue into the morning hours before this activity largely consolidates towards the coast and higher elevation areas by midday. Past 15-17z, most inland sites experience mostly dry conditions. Still, high resolution guidance hints at a slight uptick in showers inland between ~23z-04z. Dry conditions after this point outside of a lingering shower or two near the coast. Should a shower pass directly overhead, a brief period of MVFR conditions can't be ruled out - about a 10-20% chance. Looking ahead, one thing we'll definitely have to watch Monday night into Tuesday morning will be fog formation. However, confidence in the exact placement and timing was not nearly high enough to add fog as a prevailing group outside of a mention of VCFG at KEUG near the end of the TAF period. Winds today stay fairly light, generally less than 10-15 knots.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions are favored most hours today although there is a 20-25% chance to drop to MVFR 12-16z this morning. Otherwise, high confidence in VFR CIGS/VIS through the evening. Winds stay around 5-10 knots, generally out of the south. -99

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Overall impactful steep and choppy seas linger today with buoys observations in the coastal waters reporting wave heights of 19-22 ft at 13-16 seconds early this morning. Headed through the day, these seas slowly decrease decrease, ending up closer to 16-18ft come sunset. Given the conditions, a hazardous Seas Warning remains in effect across all waters, including the Columbia River Bar.

Seas are expected to subside more noticeably tonight, falling briefly into the 10-14 ft range by midday Tuesday, but this will be short lived as another system is expected to bring building seas along with a 50-70% chance of southerly Gales for locations beyond 30 NM from the coast (15-25% inner waters) late Tuesday afternoon and evening - a Gale Watch was issued for the outer waters during this time period. These increasing winds, followed by another westerly swell will result in seas re-building towards 14-17 ft range with a dominant period of 14-16 seconds by Wednesday morning.

Late week models are still in agreement on seas further diminishing, likely dropping just below 10ft on Thursday, as high pressure attempts to build overhead. As for next weekend, ensemble models hint at another storm system arrive around Saturday which would bring renewed winds and swells across all waters. -99/42

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: Hazardous high surf conditions continue today with seas currently in the 17-20 ft range. Seas of this magnitude can produce 25-30ft on our local beaches - a High Surf Advisory remains in effect through 10 AM before the seas slowly diminish. In these conditions, wave will run significantly farther up on area beaches and jetties than what is normally observed. More simply put, the sneaker wave threat will be very high. Beachgoers should use extreme caution as sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning. Never turn your back to the ocean. In addition, large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave. Further beach erosion is also possible. Avoid the beaches today if you can.
